title: Federal Judge Temporarily Blocks Border Wall in Texas' Big Bend Region
summary:
A federal court in Texas on Friday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and other infrastructure across the state's Big Bend region. The ruling is a win for landowners, businesses, and environmentalists who united against the project, which has long been a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump.

The Big Bend sector stretches roughly 500 miles — about a quarter of the 2,000-mile southern border with Mexico. The project is part of a $46 billion administration effort to add 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers, roads, and surveillance technology. The ruling covers Big Bend National Park, which sits on a bend of the Rio Grande River, and areas up and downriver.

Judge Kathleen Cardone wrote that the plaintiffs were "likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims," that they could suffer "serious, irreparable harm" without an injunction, and that the public interest favored them. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Opponents argued the region is so remote and rugged that it already deters illegal immigration. They also say the administration violated the law by issuing waivers that bypassed regulations protecting the environment, culture, and archaeology. The lawsuit was brought by an environmental organization, advocates for a historic church in Ruidosa, and a river guide.

Laiken Jordahl of the Center for Biological Diversity, which brought the suit, called the ruling a "total victory" and said bulldozers would be sent packing until the judge rules on the merits. "This is such a historic day for Big Bend and for Texas and the Constitution," Jordahl said.

The decision came weeks after the first wall panels went up in the sector in mid-September. When bulldozers cleared land in the park in August, it sparked bipartisan opposition. CBP paused work there, but that pause expired Sept. 30. The administration says it is reevaluating plans for the park.

Advocates for the park said they were happy with the ruling but called on the administration to fix the damage already done, meet with local residents, and develop alternative plans. "Big Bend is no place for border barriers," said Tiernan Sittenfeld, president and CEO of the National Parks Conservation Association.
why_it_matters: The case is a test of how far a president can go in overriding environmental and cultural laws to build border barriers, and it shows courts acting as a check on executive power — a precedent that will shape fights over public land and immigration policy for years.

background_read: Big Bend National Park sits in a remote bend of the Rio Grande — the river that marks the border between Texas and Mexico — in west Texas, and it was made a national park in 1944. It is famous for desert, mountains and deep river canyons, and it is one of the least-visited parks because it is so far from big cities.

Congress passed a law in 2005 that let the Secretary of Homeland Security waive environmental and other laws to speed up border barrier construction, a power that was used during President Donald Trump's first term. Building a wall along the southern border was a central promise of Trump's 2016 campaign, and hundreds of miles of barriers were built, much of it replacing existing fencing. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is the federal agency inside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that guards U.S. borders.

It matters that Judge Cardone's order is a preliminary injunction: it freezes the project only until she rules on the merits, so the fight is not over. The Center for Biological Diversity and the National Parks Conservation Association are advocacy groups that work to protect wildlife and national parks.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — park advocates and opponents of the wall
perspectives.description: Landowners, businesses, environmentalists and groups like the National Parks Conservation Association gained time and a legal win, arguing that even a president must follow laws protecting the environment, culture and archaeology, and that a fragile desert river ecosystem was spared.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical — the administration and wall supporters
perspectives.description: They see a lawfully funded, campaign-backed border security project being stalled by courts, leaving gaps in a sector that covers roughly a quarter of the southern border. Delay adds cost and uncertainty, and they argue the region still needs barriers and surveillance.

A preliminary injunction is not a final verdict; the judge only found the plaintiffs likely to win at least one claim. The dispute builds on a 2005 law that lets Homeland Security waive many regulations, which has been tested in court before, and border-wall litigation has historically stretched over years.

Advocates are pushing the administration to repair bulldozed land, meet with local residents and design alternatives such as technology or patrols instead of barriers. The bigger question is whether the waiver power itself will be narrowed when the case is decided on the merits.
